summary: This standards-track document specifies the IDLE command for IMAP4, which lets a client tell the server it is ready to receive real-time updates, such as new mail, without polling.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking the mailbox over and over, you wait, and it taps your shoulder when mail arrives.

questions: how to get push email with imap
how often should an imap client re-issue idle
subtitle: A command that lets an IMAP client wait while the server pushes mailbox updates in real time.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 requires a client to poll the server for changes to the selected mailbox, so new mail is not seen immediately unless the client polls very often.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends IDLE, the server answers with a continuation request, and while IDLE is active the server may send untagged EXISTS, EXPUNGE and other messages at any time. The client ends it by sending DONE.
tldr.outcome: A client can see mailbox changes right away and still only needs to re-issue IDLE at least every 29 minutes to avoid being logged off.

today: RFC 2177 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the IMAP IDLE command.

sections.title: Why IMAP Clients Had to Poll
sections.content:
The base IMAP4 protocol (RFC 2060) requires a client to poll the server for changes to the selected mailbox, such as new mail or deletions. Users would prefer to see new mail immediately, and real-time applications built on IMAP might otherwise need to poll every few seconds.

The RFC notes that the base spec does allow a server to push EXISTS responses asynchronously, but a client cannot expect this behaviour and must poll. The IDLE command lets the client say it is ready to accept such updates.
sections.eli5: Checking the mailbox again and again is tiring. IDLE lets you say, just tell me when something changes.

sections.title: How IDLE Works
sections.content:
IDLE takes no arguments. A client may use it only if the server lists IDLE in its CAPABILITY response; otherwise the client MUST NOT use it and must poll. The server answers with a continuation (+) response, and from then on it is free to send untagged EXISTS, EXPUNGE and other messages at any time.

The client ends the command by sending the continuation data DONE. The server MAY send any queued untagged responses, then MUST immediately send the tagged response to IDLE and be ready for new commands. The client MUST NOT send any other command while the server is waiting for DONE, because the server could not tell a command from a continuation. Possible results are OK, NO (the server will not allow IDLE now) and BAD.
sections.eli5: You tell the server you are listening. It can then speak up whenever something happens, and you say DONE when you want to talk again.

sections.title: Timeouts and the 29-Minute Rule
sections.content:
A server MAY consider a client with a running IDLE to be inactive, and if it has an inactivity timeout it MAY log the client off at the end of that period. Clients using IDLE are therefore advised to terminate it and re-issue it at least every 29 minutes.

This still gives immediate mailbox updates while needing to "poll" only at half hour intervals.
sections.eli5: Every so often you wave to the server to show you are still there, so it does not hang up.

sections.title: Example Session and Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC's example selects INBOX, issues A002 IDLE and gets a continuation response. New mail arrives as 4 EXISTS, then the client sends DONE and the server replies A002 OK IDLE terminated. Later, an 2 EXPUNGE from another client's deletion arrives in the same way.

The formal syntax adds idle to the commands valid in the Authenticated or Selected state, defined as "IDLE" CRLF "DONE". The RFC says there are no known security issues with this extension.
sections.eli5: The example shows the server announcing new mail all by itself while the client waits.

references.text: Crispin, M., "Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1", RFC 2060, December 1996.
